extracted.intended_audience: media studies students, journalism scholars, and newsroom professionals
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric for identifying and analyzing external (extramedia and ideological) forces that shape news and media content, including economic, community, institutional, technological, and political influences. Useful for coursework, content-audit design, and media criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripps' Constancy Hypothesis / economic support constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of economic support available (a relatively constant proportion of wealth such as GNP) constrains the growth of the mass media and dictates how the media will grow and expand (i.e., media expansion is dictated by the general economy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use economic indicators (GNP, advertising spend) as a macro-level constraint when assessing long-term media growth and resource allocation; consider that new media spending often comes at the expense of old media, keeping the overall media share of wealth roughly constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/economic conditions alter perceived newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Nationwide or industry-specific economic changes act as stimuli that cause the media to change their assessment of how newsworthy an issue is (e.g., as oil prices rise, news coverage of the oil industry increases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating coverage intensity, examine contemporaneous market indicators (prices, industry health) to explain shifts in topic salience beyond intrinsic news events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community boosterism / publisher community role
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers in small towns may act as 'community boosters,' promoting local economic development and running stories or campaigns intended to attract or support local businesses and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage serves economic development goals (e.g., promotional stories, coordinated campaigns) and whether journalists participate in booster activities (rallies, advocacy), noting examples where reporting placement differs by stance (front-page vs buried stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence versus organizational profit pressures (boosterism effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure on editorial departments to help the organization make a profit can replace detachment and objectivity with a 'team concept' that promotes the community and the firm's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate newsroom governance and evidence of editorial-business convergence (e.g., editorial choices shaped by profit motives), and look for signs of self-censorship or preferential placement for pro-community coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience/reader preferences as a driver of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Reader preferences can shape newspaper content; some newsrooms are adopting systematic methods to learn audience desires and adjust content (the 'reader-driven newspaper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for audience-research practices (surveys, focus groups, reader forums) and measure whether content changes (story length, graphics, topics) reflect those findings; contrast newsroom ignorance of audience characteristics with marketing-driven positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content audits and diversity expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Content audits (e.g., ASNE's Covering the Community) are recommended to improve local coverage, build newsroom-community ties, and encourage diversity in every story (seek diverse sources); making 'covering the total community' part of performance standards is advised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing local coverage quality, check for completed content audits, dissemination of audit reports to newsroom staff, explicit performance standards about diversity, and practices for seeking diverse sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-driven production methods and their trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques such as coupon-solicited ideas, public forums, focus groups, and mall surveys can lead to changes like fewer jumps, shorter stories, more graphics, and 'news-you-can-use,' but may limit capacity to handle complex stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate adopted reader-research techniques and their editorial consequences: check whether story depth and investigative reporting decline as space/format constraints (shorter stories, fewer jumps) increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial direction from non-local or business-minded editors
rubrics_metrics.description: More meetings and increased editorial direction (often by editors who are new to the community) can reduce reporters' time in the community and lower the barrier between editorial and business decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial staffing (local experience), frequency of editorial directives, and reporter field time; look for correlations between centralized editorial control and decline in local reporting depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Station/community content sensitivity and internal policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Local station management policies and ownership sensibilities (religious, cultural) can lead to preemptive content restrictions (e.g., affiliates dropping programs due to local sensibilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine station ownership and policy statements for content sensitivities; consider how local values or ownership guidelines translate into programming decisions or censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional affiliations and elite ideological alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors and leaders of large media corporations often share affiliations with elite institutions, creating a 'web of affiliations' that promotes a common ideology (corporate liberalism) that can shape editorial outlooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map board memberships and outside affiliations to detect ideological convergences; use these ties to explain long-term editorial shifts or organizational stances (e.g., endorsements, policy positions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocking directorates and autonomy concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Interlocks between media and nonmedia corporate boards (financial institutions, advertisers, law firms) raise questions about media firm autonomy and create potential channels for outside control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate shared directorships and cross-ownership patterns to assess potential conflicts of interest, influence over basic decisions, and vulnerability to buyouts orchestrated with financial institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependency on advertisers and other economic actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organizations' dependence on advertisers and other elite institutions can lead to content changes to avoid economic retaliation (boycotts, funding loss) and can induce self-censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging editorial independence, consider the revenue mix (advertising share), documented advertiser pressure cases, and instances where coverage softened after advertiser or funder complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-driven standardization and sameness
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological advances (mass production, distribution, standardized production processes) have led newspapers and broadcasters to standardize content across places, producing a high degree of sameness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether technological capabilities (national editions, syndicated content) have reduced local distinctiveness; examine editorial balance persistence and resistance to change once an editorial formula succeeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast technology effects on live coverage versus depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasting innovations (film to ENG, satellites, enhanced graphics) can increase live stories and better presentation of complex information but may not materially improve the informativeness or depth of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between quantity of live/visual coverage and substantive informational depth; measure whether increased live reporting corresponds to richer voter/election information or merely more coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-assisted reporting and data-driven journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of computers, databases (NEXIS, VU/TEXT), and raw data records enables journalism that identifies systemic problems and produces stories not possible without large-scale data analysis (e.g., mortgage discrimination, NTSB record analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence and effectiveness of CAR teams, usage rates among reporters, training levels (younger journalists vs veterans), and documented investigative outcomes (awards, policy changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computers reduce editing errors and improve pagination/graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic editing (VDT) and full electronic editing reduce errors (spelling, punctuation, typography); computerized pagination gives editors more control over page design and informational graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editing accuracy statistics pre- and post-adoption, adoption level of electronic pagination, and whether improved design/graphics translated into clearer storytelling rather than mere aesthetic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transnational infrastructure enables global advertising standardization
rubrics_metrics.description: A transnational communication infrastructure facilitates global advertising campaigns and 'one standard message' that overcomes language and literacy barriers via internationally recognized visual symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing content homogenization and advertising influence, consider the role of global media networks and standardized ad formats in reducing local cultural specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence and multimedia corporate alliances reshape content production
rubrics_metrics.description: Alliances among electronic networks, newspapers, software firms, and telecoms (e.g., Prodigy with Times Mirror, Oracle with Washington Post) enable interactive, multimedia news and advertising, altering what content can be produced and how it is monetized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine corporate partnerships and platform strategies to understand new content forms (interactive, multimedia) and monetization models (subscription, integrated ads) that may influence editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel proliferation may lower standards and increase sensational content
rubrics_metrics.description: A predicted proliferation of cable channels will create more time slots to fill, which may reduce standards and increase violent or low-quality content as providers fill inventory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the supply-demand pressures of many channels when evaluating programming quality; look for content dilution or sensationalism correlating with channel supply increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest-group influence and the mixed success of organized pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups organize to influence media content (press guidelines, campaigns), but their success is mixed; those able to retaliate economically (consumer boycotts) are more likely to affect coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the methods interest groups use (guidelines, boycotts) and their capacities for economic retaliation; examine case studies where retaliation led to content changes or where guidelines had limited effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations tactics (pseudoevents) as a content control strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of pseudoevents by public relations practitioners is a way to control media content by manufacturing newsworthy occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating source-driven content, identify events that are staged or orchestrated for media coverage (press conferences, photo-ops) and analyze their prevalence and effect on agenda-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience commodification and advertisers' direct content interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences are valuable because attention is sold to advertisers; advertisers often influence content and increasingly produce advertiser-created programming or integrate commercials to prevent ad-avoidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the extent of advertiser-produced content, integrated advertising strategies (unskippable ads), and how commercial imperatives shape editorial boundaries and children's programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental legal and regulatory controls over media content and ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments influence media via laws (e.g., libel) and regulations determining who can own broadcast media and what content is permitted; level of control varies by country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the regulatory environment (ownership rules, content restrictions, libel law enforcement) to account for legal constraints on editorial decisions and ownership structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market structure effects: market size, economic health, and competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketplace characteristics—market size, profit opportunities, and overall economic health—affect content; however, competition does not necessarily increase diversity and may have negative effects such as sensationalism or sabotage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing pluralism and diversity, go beyond number of outlets to study market incentives, ownership concentration, and how competition manifests (quality rivalry vs trivial one-upmanship).
